🌐 President Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented trilateral gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers. Keep reading.
 
 
1 big thing: America stops
 
Flightradar24, a global flight tracking service, posted this snapshot of 3,100 aircraft bound for U.S. airports as the nationwide ground stop began. Image: Flightradar24 via X

The chaos from the FAA's nationwide ground stop continues today, with nearly 3,500 flights already canceled as airlines played catch-up.

  • Why it matters: Millions of travelers will be inconvenienced over what the government says was simply old technology that couldn't keep up with modern upgrades.

The Friday the 13th ground stop, the longest since 9/11, lasted 4 hours, 21 minutes — from 3:54 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. ET.

  • FlightAware reported more than 6,000 cancellations yesterday. Passengers waiting for rebooking formed huge lines in airport lounges.

At a White House briefing last night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was issued after outdated air traffic control communications equipment suffered from "overloaded data, and they went down."

  • Duffy said the problems weren't linked to a new AI-powered system the FAA is rolling out: "This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that's been deployed did not go down."
  • Duffy spent much of the press conference pushing Congress for more funding — $50 billion — for upgrades. He said similar problems could occur again without more money.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin added that officials are looking into incompatibilities between that older equipment and newer technology currently being installed.

  • Mullin said there's no evidence that the problems were tied to a cyberattack.

But Duffy and Mullin didn't specify the exact initial cause of the problems.

2. 🏈 Flightmare jumbles college kickoffs
 

Covers of today's New York Post and California Post.

 

The nationwide ground stop left NBA, NHL and college teams scrambling to reach their destinations in time for this weekend's games.

  • No. 19 Mississippi's football game at Oklahoma was moved from today to Sunday, usually reserved for the NFL, at 1 p.m. EST. The SEC said the Ole Miss football team couldn't leave Oxford last night and will travel this afternoon.
  • Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny ripped the decision, saying the SEC threatened Oklahoma with a forfeit if it didn't agree to the move. Go deeper.

⏱️ Lots of today's kickoff times are changing. Most college football teams travel the day before their game, and several teams returned to campus from the airport, AP reports.

  • Auburn opted to take a bus to Mississippi State, with the SEC pushing back today's start time from noon EST to 4:15 p.m. to give the Tigers a little buffer. Purdue likewise decided to board buses from West Lafayette, Indiana, for its game at Iowa.

NFL teams playing Sunday typically travel the day before their games. They were expected to fly as planned today.

3. 🤖 AI's trust collapse
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

President Trump handed AI titans an extraordinary mandate six weeks ago: Police yourselves.

  • But the industry faces a four-pronged crisis of trust as Democrats surge to power and many Americans rebel over AI and data centers, Axios' Erica Pandey reports.
  • Guardrails for the industry will be a priority for the new Congress, with some populist Republicans eager to pile on.

The big picture: Trump announced in late September that top AI CEOs had agreed to a voluntary safety accord. Since then, four crises have converged:

🏛️ 1. The political crisis: AI was on the ballot for the first time during the midterm elections through a series of data center measures across America. People voted against data centers in 40 out of 41 cases, and swing-state incumbents linked to the facilities, including Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), were voted out.

  • Democrats are planning to unleash a flood of AI bills when they take control of Congress in January. They'll also bring some of the most powerful AI executives to D.C. to testify.

🦺 2. The safety crisis: OpenAI's Hugging Face breach, revealed in July, was a terrifying look at what could happen if machines operate beyond humans' control — and it was the first in a wave of revelations through the summer and fall.

  • AI CEOs and engineers came forward with stark warnings about the dangers of the tech they've been building, including its potential to destroy humanity.

💰 3. The financial crisis: The AI trade is looking more vulnerable as investors question when or whether the industry's sky-high spending will deliver sky-high returns.

  • Tech stocks tumbled, with Nvidia falling 13% this week amid the ouster of founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The stock has lost nearly 25% of its value since the first New York Times report in late October about Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy.

🧐 4. The leadership crisis: Huang's stunning resignation is raising new questions about the vulnerability of the people running America's most powerful companies.

  • Pop culture has turned on the AI titans, with three year-end films — "The Social Reckoning" and "Musk," out last month, and "Artificial," opening Christmas Day — savaging Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

4. 🚀 Starship soars despite diversion
 
The booster of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 explodes after launching yesterday from Starbase, Texas. Photo: Ricardo Arduengo via Getty Images

SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded yesterday. But the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.

  • Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster was diverted to a point offshore. Despite the setback, the spacecraft continued on its way.

5. 🥕 Fresh inflation fears
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

Americans are already paying more for groceries — and new inflation data this week suggests that the pressure is not letting up, Axios' Courtenay Brown reports.

  • The latest: Food prices are rising sharply even before they reach supermarket shelves.

📈 Wholesale fresh and dry vegetable prices surged 27% last month, adding to a 31% price jump the previous month.

  • These are the prices paid by food distributors, grocery chains and other businesses to farmers and other producers for eventual sale to consumers.

Zoom in: Unusually warm weather, crop disease and insect infestations have reduced lettuce and other leafy green harvests in California.

  • The Iran war has driven up the cost of fertilizer and fuel, making it more expensive to grow and transport food.

🥬 Case in point: A regional grocery chain recently told Fed officials that it now costs more to transport a head of lettuce from California than to buy the lettuce itself, citing high diesel fuel prices.

  • Go deeper: High transportation costs drive wholesale prices.
 
 
6. 🇨🇳 MAGA turns on Lutnick
 
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick steps off Marine One and walks into the White House last Sunday. Photo: Joey Sussman/ZUMA Press

Commerce Secretary Lutnick has become the face of the Trump administration's troubled response to Chinese espionage and potential national security threats, Axios' Maria Curi and Marc Caputo report.

  • The most intense scrutiny is coming from Republicans on the Hill, fellow Cabinet members and the MAGA base.

Why it matters: Regulators and policymakers on both sides of the aisle want someone's head for an affair that may have exposed sensitive technology to the nation's top foreign adversary.

  • Two names are currently at the top of that list: former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — and now Howard Lutnick.

7. 🌆 It's "Grand Theft Auto VI" week
 
A screenshot of Vice City from "Grand Theft Auto VI." Photo: Rockstar Games

We're five days away from "Grand Theft Auto VI" going live, and the madness may be unlike anything we've seen before, Axios' Herb Scribner writes.

  • "GTA VI" has been in development for nearly 15 years and is shaping up to be the year's biggest cultural phenomenon. Millions of Americans are already planning on skipping work so they can drive around in slick cars and commit virtual crimes.

The game, which cost Rockstar Games more than $2 billion to make, has already earned more than $1 billion from preorders.

🚗 The new "Grand Theft Auto" finally arrives Thursday. Pre-loading of the 212 GB files began last week.

  • The buzz is off the charts. The game has already sold at least 11 million copies, per Sensor Tower.

Launch gallery
 
 
8. ❄️ 1 for the road: White Thanksgiving
 
Map: The Old Farmer's Almanac via Reuters

Rain, snow and wintry weather could complicate holiday travel during Thanksgiving week. Parts of the Upper Midwest and Northeast could see snow, according to The Old Farmer's Almanac's November forecast.

  • The forecast for Thanksgiving Day itself is milder across much of the country, but Midwesterners might be in for a white Thanksgiving.
